clue.text: Brass groom spent on foremost of dinners and a buffet

indicators.note: on places the next letter after the rearranged block
spent suggests worn out and knocked out of shape, so the letters of brass and groom are rearranged
foremost of takes only the leading letter of dinners

explanation.surface: A stable lad, having blown his money on fine dinners, ends up at a cheap buffet.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian spread of many dishes laid out for guests to help themselves is a buffet.

clue.text: Favourite's upset privately to make room for a replacement

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word above it upside down, so the letters of the favourite's word read backwards

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, and the possessive adds an S
aside means privately, as in a remark spoken aside

explanation.surface: The favourite in a race is upset and quietly withdraws so a substitute can run.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw from a position so that someone else can take it over is the idiom meant.

clue.text: Extra owed is yet to arrive

parts.note: over means extra or remaining, as in left over
money owed is due

explanation.surface: An additional sum that is owed has still not been paid in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something late, past its expected time, has not yet arrived.

clue.text: Crack crackers and become very angry

parts.note: a crack at something is an attempt, a go
crackers and bananas are both slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Someone snaps open Christmas crackers and loses their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Both crack and crackers look like the same idea; each is a separate piece, one a noun for an attempt and one an adjective for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal idiom means to lose one's temper wildly, to rage.

clue.text: Grass-like plant in small border

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A grassy plant grows in a narrow garden border.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a tufted marsh plant that looks like grass but belongs to a different family.

clue.text: Famous actor, one in 'Cromwell', for example

indicators.note: in means the numeral letter goes inside the first name

parts.note: Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector, is an example of an Oliver
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A celebrated actor takes a part in a film called Cromwell.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make Cromwell look like a film title, but it stands for Oliver Cromwell, the 17th-century English ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence, the English stage and screen star, is one of the most famous actors of the 20th century.

clue.text: Put off, cleaner gent jilted

indicators.note: jilted means thrown over, so the man named is dropped from the cleaner

parts.note: a detergent is a cleaning agent
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady is put off after a gentleman abandons her.
explanation.definitionFit: To discourage someone from acting is to put them off.

clue.text: Girl from Lancashire (Nelson)

indicators.note: from says the name is taken out of the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A young woman comes from Nelson, a town in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: The name straddles the end of Lancashire and the start of Nelson. Nelson is a mill town in Lancashire, a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a woman's first name, and crosswords use girl for any such name.

clue.text: Elected charitable trust with perfect sincerity

parts.note: a politician who is elected is in office
a charitable deed is a good one
faith means trust or belief

explanation.surface: An elected official sets up a charity trust and means it honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: Charitable trust reads as one legal term, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting honestly, without intent to deceive, is the idiom meant.

clue.text: Wicked (excellent) playing game

parts.note: bad means wicked
mint means in excellent, perfect condition
a show that is on is playing

explanation.surface: A player praises a wicked, excellent match in slang terms.
explanation.walkthrough: Wicked and excellent are both slang for great, which leads one to read them as one idea.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a racket sport played over a high net with a shuttlecock.

clue.text: Being this causes a problem seeing the reading's wrong

definitions.text: Being this causes a problem seeing

indicators.note: wrong suggests letters gone awry, so the words before it are rearranged

parts.note: the apostrophe S here is a contraction of is, and its S letter counts

explanation.surface: Someone blames poor eyesight for misreading text.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the three words before 'wrong', the S included.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-sighted people cannot see distant things clearly, which causes problems with vision.

clue.text: A theologian in valley brings cheer

indicators.note: in puts the article and the theologian inside the valley

parts.note: a glen is a narrow valley, especially in Scotland
DD stands for Doctor of Divinity, a theologian

explanation.surface: A churchman living in a valley lifts people's spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone happy is to cheer them, used here as a verb.

clue.text: Retire abroad, going to a country in Africa

indicators.note: abroad can mean all over the place, so the letters of retire are scattered

explanation.surface: Someone retiring overseas moves to an African nation.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a nation on the Red Sea coast in the Horn of Africa, with Asmara its capital.

clue.text: Extremely nice, after work, I suppose

indicators.note: after places the outer letters of nice behind the other pieces

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a musical work

indicators.note: extremely takes the extremes, the outer letters, of nice

explanation.surface: Someone muses that something will be very pleasant once work is done.
explanation.definitionFit: To give an opinion, to suppose or state a view, is the sense.

clue.text: Row with senior sorted? That's OK

indicators.note: sorted means put in order, so the letters of row and senior are rearranged

explanation.surface: A quarrel with an elder is settled, and all is well.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian-style reassurance means everything is fine, don't worry about it.

clue.text: Yield after a powerful blow?

parts.note: fruit knocked from trees by a strong wind is a crop or yield brought down by a gust; the word also means an unexpected gain

explanation.walkthrough: Blow looks like a punch, but it is a gust of wind, and yield is the harvest of apples it brings down.
explanation.definitionFit: These are fruits blown off a tree by the wind, and by extension any unexpected gain.

clue.text: Fashionable, even, like nurses on the wards?

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing
uniform means even or consistent

explanation.surface: Hospital nurses look smart and consistent in their dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospital nurses wear standard work outfits, so they are dressed alike.

clue.text: Society member's unusual forenames

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of forenames come in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A member of a club has strange first names.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a member of a fraternal secret society known for its lodges and rituals.

clue.text: French solver playing ragtime

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of ragtime are toyed with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A French puzzle fan is playing some ragtime music.
explanation.walkthrough: Solver looks like a crossword fan, but here it means a solver of crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Simenon's fictional Paris police inspector solves crimes, so he is a French detective.

clue.text: Amaze leader of gang, being taken for a ride

parts.note: to stun is to amaze

indicators.note: leader of takes the first letter of gang

explanation.surface: A gang boss is astonished at being driven off somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Being taken for a ride means being cheated, and someone swindled has been stung.

clue.text: Warehousing charge could be so great

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters of so great might be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A fee for keeping goods in a warehouse might be enormous.
explanation.definitionFit: The fee paid for keeping goods in a depot is called by the same word as the keeping itself.

clue.text: Urgent-looking letters in capitals I scrawled Pa sent back crossed out

indicators.note: scrawled means written messily, so the remaining letters are jumbled
crossed out says the reversed father is struck from capitals
sent back means the two letters of the father are read backwards

parts.note: pa is father

explanation.surface: Someone wrote in capitals, then crossed out what was sent back to their father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns PA into AP; 'crossed out' takes AP from CAPITALS, leaving CITALS; 'scrawled' mixes CITALS and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloping type is used for emphasis, so it looks urgent on the page.

clue.text: Metal block in Victorian village

indicators.note: in says the answer is inside the run of letters of the two words

explanation.surface: There is an iron block in an old Victorian village smithy.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith hammers metal on this heavy iron block.

clue.text: Large firm

definitions.meaning: a large drink, a ... whisky, is a strong measure

explanation.definitionFit: A stiff drink is a large, strong one, and something rigid is firm.

clue.text: Primate taken in by newspaper seller in the high street?

indicators.note: taken in by says the primate goes inside the newspaper

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper
a loris is a small primate

explanation.surface: A monkey gets fooled by a newsagent on the high street.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken in looks like deceived but means put inside. 'High' is a joke: plants and flowers grow high.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper who sells cut flowers and bouquets trades on a typical town shopping street.

clue.text: Dither on rising ground in Suffolk town

indicators.note: on puts one piece next to the other, joined as one word

parts.note: to haver is to dither or hesitate
a hill is rising ground

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates on a slope in Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town lies in south-west Suffolk, an English county in East Anglia.

clue.text: Very keen to employ old dodge

indicators.note: to employ means to take on, so the eager word holds the abbreviation inside

parts.note: avid means very keen

explanation.surface: An eager boss hires an old worker to evade something.
explanation.definitionFit: To evade or sidestep something is to dodge it.

clue.text: Released pent-up emotions, then forgave second XI, perhaps

parts.note: to let someone off is to forgive them
XI, eleven players, is an example of a team

explanation.surface: A coach vented anger, then forgave the reserve side.
explanation.walkthrough: Second XI looks like the reserve side, but it splits into S for second and a team, an XI being eleven players.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from steam engines venting pressure, means to release built-up feelings.
